Footnote: from camp on Steep Lake to Beartrack Lake is about 1 hour travel time with one portage at each lake.

surveys.narrative:
Temperature and dissolved oxygen (DO) measurements were collected from the deepest basin in Steep Lake on August 5th, 2024, to evaluate the quantity and quality of cold, oxygenated water (i.e., oxythermal habitat) available to Cisco, also known as Tullibee, the most sensitive coldwater species present in this lake. During the summer, Cisco require a layer of oxythermal habitat that contains water temperatures below 21.2 degrees C (70.2 degrees F) and dissolved oxygen concentrations above 3.0 mg/L. Based on the profile from the deepest basin (maximum sampled depth 33.1 feet), the water temperature decreased below 21.2 degrees C (70.2 degrees F) at 14.1 feet and the dissolved oxygen concentration decreased to 3.0 mg/L at 19.3 feet at the time of sampling. The thickness of this layer of water in the water column was 5.2 feet, indicating that oxythermal habitat was present for Cisco.

Further, the temperature at which dissolved oxygen decreased to 3.0 mg/L (i.e., TDO3, a single variable to characterize oxythermal habitat) was 14.6 degrees C (58.3 degrees F). TDO3 values cooler than 21.2 degrees C (70.2 degrees F) indicate that oxythermal conditions were suitable for Cisco at the time of the survey.

Data collected by the Minnesota Department of Natural Resources during the late summer period of maximum oxythermal stress (July 26th to Aug 24th) in 2018 also indicates suitable oxythermal habitat. When inadequate oxythermal habitat is available, Cisco are squeezed into unfavorable, warmer water conditions and experience higher levels of stress.

Steep is a small, clear-water lake located in the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness. The lake is only accessible via portage trails coming from Eugene or South Lakes. There are two primitive campsites maintained by the U.S. Forest Service on the lake.

The fish community was simple and only four species were sampled in 2018, which was the same number sampled in the previous survey (1974). However, the composition changed; in 2018, Northern Pike were absent and Green Sunfish were present for the first time. Cisco, Rock Bass, and White Sucker were present in both surveys, but sizes were small. In 1965, 13,689 Ohrid Trout (Salmo letnica) were stocked as fingerlings, however, none were ever captured in any of the assessments.

Steep is a beautiful lake for paddling, camping or swimming but better fishing can be found in some of the neighboring lakes.

Temperature and dissolved oxygen (DO) measurements were collected from the deepest basin in Steep Lake on July 30th, 2025, to evaluate the quantity and quality of cold, oxygenated water (i.e., oxythermal habitat) available to Cisco, also known as Tullibee, the most sensitive coldwater species present in this lake. During the summer, Cisco require a layer of oxythermal habitat that contains water temperatures below 21.2 degrees C (70.2 degrees F) and dissolved oxygen concentrations above 3.0 mg/L. Based on the profile from the deepest basin (maximum sampled depth 32.8 feet), the water temperature decreased below 21.2 degrees C (70.2 degrees F) at 14.1 feet and the dissolved oxygen concentration decreased to 3.0 mg/L at 22.7 feet at the time of sampling. The thickness of this layer of water in the water column was 8.7 feet, indicating that oxythermal habitat was present for Cisco.

Further, the temperature at which dissolved oxygen decreased to 3.0 mg/L (i.e., TDO3, a single variable to characterize oxythermal habitat) was 10.1 degrees C (50.2 degrees F). TDO3 values cooler than 21.2 degrees C (70.2 degrees F) indicate that oxythermal conditions were suitable for Cisco at the time of the survey.

Data collected by the Minnesota Department of Natural Resources during the late summer period of maximum oxythermal stress (July 26th to Aug 24th) in 2018 and 2024 also indicate suitable oxythermal habitat in all years surveyed. The least favorable conditions were recorded in 2024 when the suitable oxythermal habitat layer was 5.2 feet thick. When inadequate oxythermal habitat is available, Cisco are squeezed into unfavorable, warmer water conditions and experience higher levels of stress.
